lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: The Nitrogen Cycle as a Repeated Pattern in Nature

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Identify the nitrogen cycle from the internet, charts or pictures.
- Explain the nitrogen cycle depicting processes such as nitrogen fixation, nitrification, assimilation, ammonification and denitrification.
- Explain the relationship between the nitrogen cycle and the environment.
- Explain why the nitrogen cycle is a repeated pattern in nature.

pages.title: Why Living Things Need Nitrogen
pages.body: Nitrogen is an element every living thing needs to build proteins, genetic material and other essential compounds, yet the nitrogen gas that makes up about four fifths of the air around us cannot be used directly by most plants and animals. The nitrogen cycle is the continuous movement of nitrogen between the atmosphere, the soil, and living organisms, converting unusable nitrogen gas into forms that plants can absorb, passing that nitrogen along to animals, and eventually returning it to the atmosphere so the whole process can begin again.

questions.q: The nitrogen cycle is best described as
o: A one way process that never repeats
The complete destruction of nitrogen over time
The continuous movement of nitrogen between the atmosphere, soil and living things
The formation of new nitrogen atoms from oxygen
questions.e: The nitrogen cycle is the continuous movement of nitrogen between the atmosphere, the soil, and living organisms, converting unusable nitrogen gas into forms that plants can absorb, passing that nitrogen along to animals, and eventually returning it to the…

pages.title: Nitrogen Fixation
pages.body: Nitrogen fixation is the process by which nitrogen gas in the air is converted into a form plants can use, mainly ammonia or related nitrogen compounds. This conversion is carried out mostly by nitrogen fixing bacteria, some of which live freely in the soil, and others of which live in small swellings called root nodules found on the roots of leguminous plants, such as beans and groundnuts, in a mutually beneficial partnership with the plant. A smaller amount of nitrogen fixation also happens naturally through lightning, which provides enough energy to force nitrogen gas to react with oxygen in the air, forming nitrogen compounds that are washed into the soil by rain.

pages.title: Nitrification
pages.body: Nitrification is the process by which ammonia, produced during nitrogen fixation, is converted first into nitrites and then into nitrates by specific soil bacteria, commonly called nitrifying bacteria. Nitrates are the form of nitrogen that plant roots absorb most readily, which is why nitrification is such an essential step, turning the products of nitrogen fixation into a form plants can directly take up and use to build proteins and grow.

questions.q: Nitrogen fixation is the process by which
o: Ammonia is converted into nitrates
Dead matter releases ammonia into soil
Nitrates are converted back into nitrogen gas
Nitrogen gas is converted into a usable form such as ammonia
questions.e: Nitrogen fixation is the process by which nitrogen gas in the air is converted into a form plants can use, mainly ammonia or related nitrogen compounds.

pages.title: Assimilation
pages.body: Assimilation is the process by which plants absorb nitrates (or, in some cases, ammonium compounds) from the soil through their roots and use this nitrogen to build proteins, chlorophyll and genetic material within their own cells. When animals eat plants, or eat other animals that have eaten plants, they in turn assimilate this same nitrogen into their own bodies, which is how nitrogen originally taken from the air by bacteria eventually becomes part of the muscles, organs and genetic material of humans and other animals.

pages.title: Ammonification
pages.body: Ammonification is the process by which decomposers, mainly bacteria and fungi, break down the nitrogen containing compounds found in dead plants, dead animals and animal waste, releasing the nitrogen back into the soil in the form of ammonia or ammonium compounds. This decayed nitrogen can then re enter the cycle through nitrification, being converted once again into nitrates that plants can absorb, showing how the cycle continually recycles nitrogen already present in the environment rather than requiring fresh nitrogen fixation every time.

o: Bacteria converting nitrates into nitrogen gas
Dead matter decomposing in the soil
Nitrogen escaping into the atmosphere
Plants and animals using absorbed nitrogen to build proteins and other compounds
questions.e: Assimilation is the process by which plants absorb nitrates (or, in some cases, ammonium compounds) from the soil through their roots and use this nitrogen to build proteins, chlorophyll and genetic material within their own cells.

pages.title: Denitrification
pages.body:
Denitrification is the process by which certain soil bacteria, called denitrifying bacteria, convert nitrates in the soil back into nitrogen gas, which then escapes into the atmosphere. Denitrification typically happens in waterlogged or oxygen poor soils, where these particular bacteria thrive, and it completes the nitrogen cycle by returning nitrogen to the air, ready to be fixed once again by nitrogen fixing bacteria or lightning.

[[pic:A circular flow diagram showing the nitrogen cycle, with the atmosphere (nitrogen gas) at the top, arrows labelled Nitrogen fixation leading down to soil ammonia, then Nitrification leading to nitrates, then Assimilation leading into a plant and an animal, then Ammonification leading from dead matter back to soil ammonia, and Denitrification leading from soil nitrates back up to the atmosphere, completing the loop.]]

Notice how the arrows in the cycle form a continuous loop, with nitrogen fixation and denitrification acting as the two gateways between the atmosphere and the soil, while nitrification, assimilation and ammonification move nitrogen between the soil, plants, animals and back to the soil again.

pages.title: The Nitrogen Cycle and the Environment
pages.body: The nitrogen cycle maintains a natural balance of nitrogen compounds in the soil and the atmosphere that supports healthy plant growth across entire ecosystems, without any single organism needing to supply all the nitrogen itself. Soil fertility depends heavily on a properly functioning nitrogen cycle, since plants cannot grow well in nitrogen poor soil, and the animals and humans that depend on those plants for food are affected in turn. Human activities can disturb this natural balance, for example when excess nitrogen fertiliser washes into rivers and lakes, encouraging excessive growth of algae that can harm aquatic life, or when the destruction of leguminous plants and natural bush reduces the amount of nitrogen fixation taking place in an area.

lessons.title: Why the Nitrogen Cycle is a Repeated Pattern

pages.title: Why the Nitrogen Cycle is a Repeated Pattern
pages.body: The nitrogen cycle is described as a repeated pattern of change because the same sequence of processes, fixation, nitrification, assimilation, ammonification and denitrification, keeps happening again and again, moving the same nitrogen atoms endlessly between the atmosphere, the soil, plants and animals. Nitrogen is never created or destroyed in this process, only converted from one chemical form to another and passed from one part of the environment to the next, in much the same way the carbon cycle, studied in an earlier grade, continually recycles carbon rather than using it up.

pages.title: The Processes of the Nitrogen Cycle and the Organisms Responsible
pages.body:
| **PROCESS** | **WHAT HAPPENS** | **WHAT BRINGS IT ABOUT** |
|---|---|---|
| **Nitrogen fixation** | Nitrogen gas from the air is changed into nitrogen compounds that plants can use | Rhizobium bacteria in the root nodules of legumes, free living bacteria in the soil such as Azotobacter, and lightning |
| **Absorption and feeding** | Plants take in nitrates through their roots and use them to make proteins. Animals get nitrogen by eating plants or other animals | Plant roots and feeding by animals |
| **Ammonification, or decay** | Proteins in dead plants and animals, and urea in animal waste, are changed into ammonia and ammonium compounds | Decomposers, which are bacteria and fungi |
| **Nitrification** | Ammonium compounds are changed first into nitrites and then into nitrates | Nitrosomonas bacteria form nitrites and Nitrobacter bacteria form nitrates |
| **Denitrification** | Nitrates in the soil are changed back into nitrogen gas, which returns to the air | Denitrifying bacteria, which are most active in waterlogged soil that lacks air |

About 78 percent of the air is nitrogen gas, but plants and animals cannot use nitrogen in this form. The nitrogen cycle is the only natural way in which nitrogen from the air becomes available to living things and is later returned to the air.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Farmers can take practical advantage of the nitrogen cycle by practising crop rotation, deliberately planting leguminous crops such as beans, groundnuts or cowpea between seasons of other crops such as maize. Since the root nodules of leguminous plants host nitrogen fixing bacteria, this practice naturally restores nitrogen to the soil without relying only on manufactured fertiliser, illustrating how understanding a natural cycle can directly inform good agricultural practice.

Producing large amounts of nitrogen gas directly

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Importance of the Nitrogen Cycle to the Environment

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Describe the importance of nitrogen to the environment.
- Carry out a project to show how certain plants such as leguminous crops can replenish nitrogen in the soil.
- Predict what will happen if the nitrogen cycle is interrupted by actions such as leaching, bush burning, and destruction of leguminous plants.

pages.title: Why Nitrogen Matters to the Environment
pages.body: Building proteins for growth, supporting soil fertility, and sustaining entire food chains are three broad reasons nitrogen is essential to the environment, building directly on the nitrogen cycle process studied in Lesson 1. Every living cell needs nitrogen to build proteins and genetic material, which is why a shortage of usable nitrogen in an ecosystem limits how well plants can grow, how well animals that depend on those plants can feed, and ultimately how productive an entire environment can be.

questions.q: Nitrogen is essential to the environment mainly because it is needed to
o: Build proteins and genetic material in living cells
Cool the atmosphere directly
Provide oxygen for respiration
Replace water in living cells
questions.e: Nitrogen is an element every living thing needs to build proteins, genetic material and other essential compounds, yet the nitrogen gas that makes up about four fifths of the air around us cannot be used directly by most plants and animals.

pages.title: Nitrogen and Soil Fertility
pages.body: Soil fertility depends heavily on the amount of usable nitrogen, mainly in the form of nitrates, available to plant roots. Fertile soil, rich in nitrogen compounds produced through nitrogen fixation and nitrification, supports vigorous plant growth, larger leaves, and healthier crops. Poor soil, depleted of nitrogen, produces stunted, yellowing plants that struggle to grow well, which is why farmers pay close attention to maintaining nitrogen levels in their fields, whether through natural means or added fertiliser.

pages.title: Replenishing Soil Nitrogen with Leguminous Plants
pages.body:
Leguminous plants, such as beans, groundnuts, cowpea and soybean, offer farmers a natural, low cost way to replenish nitrogen in depleted soil, because of the nitrogen fixing bacteria housed in their root nodules. Growing a leguminous crop, then ploughing its remains back into the soil after harvest, or simply allowing its roots to remain in the ground, adds a significant amount of nitrogen compounds to the soil, ready to support the next crop planted in that field. A simple project to demonstrate this involves planting a leguminous crop in one plot and a non leguminous crop, such as maize, in a similar plot with the same soil, then comparing the growth and yield of a subsequent crop planted in each plot.

[[pic:Two side by side photographs or drawings comparing plant growth, one showing healthy, tall, green maize plants growing in soil previously planted with beans, and the other showing shorter, paler maize plants growing in soil that had no leguminous crop grown beforehand, with a caption explaining the nitrogen difference.]]

Notice how the visible difference in plant health between the two plots reflects the underlying difference in soil nitrogen content, providing clear, practical evidence of how leguminous crops replenish nitrogen through the processes described in Lesson 1.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: What Happens When the Nitrogen Cycle is Interrupted

pages.title: What Happens When the Nitrogen Cycle is Interrupted
pages.body:
Leaching, bush burning and the destruction of leguminous plants are three human related disturbances that can interrupt the nitrogen cycle and reduce the amount of usable nitrogen available in an environment.

- Leaching occurs when heavy rainfall washes soluble nitrate compounds down through the soil, beyond the reach of plant roots, and eventually into groundwater or rivers, removing nitrogen from the topsoil where plants need it most and potentially polluting water sources.

- Bush burning destroys organic matter and the nitrogen fixing bacteria living within it, releasing stored nitrogen compounds as gases into the atmosphere rather than allowing them to remain in the soil, and repeated burning over time can leave soil increasingly nitrogen poor.

- Destruction of leguminous plants, whether through clearing land for other uses or through overharvesting without replacement, removes an important natural source of nitrogen fixation from an area, reducing the amount of new nitrogen entering the soil through this pathway.

If these disturbances continue over time, soil in the affected area is likely to become progressively less fertile, supporting weaker plant growth, lower crop yields, and, over the longer term, a decline in the overall productivity of the local environment, since every other organism in the food chain ultimately depends on nitrogen first being made available to plants.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Understanding the importance of the nitrogen cycle has led to sustainable farming practices around the world, including crop rotation with legumes, reduced tillage to protect soil bacteria, and careful, measured use of nitrogen fertiliser to avoid the water pollution problems linked to excess nitrogen leaching into rivers and lakes. These practices show that protecting a natural cycle can go hand in hand with productive, profitable farming.
